findings.where: First screen at phone width (390 px): the order of the heading, the yellow address strip and the supporting paragraph
findings.fault: On a phone, the line that says what Mark does and for whom ('I advise multilateral development banks, development agencies and governments on infrastructure…') comes after the yellow 'Write to me directly' strip, so it falls below the first phone screen. That screen shows his name, the World Bank line, the photo and a general opinion about PPPs, then asks the visitor to write before telling them what he offers. On desktop the paragraph comes before the action. On the phone it reads as an afterthought trailing the contact strip, inside the frame.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer who opens the site on a phone from a LinkedIn link. In the first five seconds they cannot tell that Mark advises banks and governments, and they are asked to email him before they know whether he is relevant. The founder would also object, because the first screen is meant to give one message and then one action, in that order.

findings.where: Article specimen, the 'Download' block at the foot of the article: the lecture title and its 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF' line
findings.fault: The download sits in the article's column straight after the article's last line, with nothing setting it apart. That placement says it is this article's PDF, but it is a different piece: a 2026 lecture under a 2024 blog post. On desktop, its own date-and-type line is pushed to the far right edge, away from the title it describes, so the label drifts loose from the thing it labels.
findings.who_objects: A reader who finishes the blog post and clicks 'Download' expecting the post as a PDF, then gets an unrelated lecture. Angélique, who will copy this pattern when adding articles, would also be left unsure whether a download belongs to its article or is a separate item.
